Russia’s Central Bank Authorizes Sberbank to Exchange Cryptocurrencies

Sberbank will debut its bitcoin-related products in December.

Russia’s Central Bank Authorizes Sberbank to Exchange Cryptocurrencies

Russia’s central bank has added Sberbank to its register of organizations authorized to exchange digital currencies, according to reports. 

Sberbank was added to the list of digital depositories, which will keep a record of cryptocurrencies and digital rights, earlier this month. 

Now, it joins eight other organizations on the exchange register, including state-controlled VTB, Russia’s second-largest bank, and T-Invest Lab, part of T-Technologies, which also owns online lender T-Bank, according to a Monday report from Interfax. 

The announcement comes as Russia fast moves forward with Bitcoin-related regulation. Sberbank last month announced that it was the first in the country to have been approved to custody bitcoin. 

The Bank of Russia gave it the green light for “digital currency record-keeping” and to facilitate the transfer of such assets, covering bitcoin and other, smaller cryptocurrencies. 

“This status will allow the bank to provide services related to organizing the circulation of digital currency on interfaces which clients already use,” Sberbank was quoted saying in the news report. 

A law on digital currencies and digital rights came into effect in Russia on September 1, creating a comprehensive legal framework for cryptocurrency circulation. Transactions involving cryptocurrencies can be conducted via the existing infrastructure of exchanges, brokers and trustees, and now also via crypto exchanges and digital depositories. 

Cryptocurrency can be bought and sold via crypto exchanges, while the rights to these assets are recorded in digital depositories.

Banks and other organizations have been able to apply to the CBR for the corresponding licenses since October 5. Some existing players have simplified access to the market and can obtain licenses on a notification basis within just one day.

Under the new rules, unqualified investors will be able to buy bitcoin and other cryptocurrencies including stablecoins, within a limit of 300,000 rubles ($3,556) per year through one intermediary. 

Qualified investors will have access to all cryptocurrencies traded on the exchange and over-the-counter markets.

Sberbank will debut its crypto wallet in December — the same month the Moscow Exchange will debut crypto trading.

The Undercurrent: Three European Artists on Making Money Visible

Amsterdam helped lay the foundations of modern finance, but its artists were among its earliest critics. When speculative bubbles burst across Europe in 1720, Amsterdam printers and satirists responded with The Great Mirror of Folly, a collection of engravings and plays exposing the excesses of financial speculation.

Nearly three centuries later, the city hosted another monetary experiment. David Chaum, the cryptographer whose work on anonymous communication helped lay the groundwork for the cypherpunk movement, came to Amsterdam in the 1980s to work at CWI, the Dutch national research institute for mathematics and computer science. Around 1990, he founded DigiCash to develop private electronic cash. The company went bankrupt in 1998, a decade before bitcoin, but the dream of digital money was already taking shape.

Last year at Bitcoin Amsterdam, BMAG exhibited The Waterworks of Money, in which Dutch artist Carlijn Kingma, working with financial journalist Thomas Bollen and researcher Martijn Jeroen van der Linden, depicted the monetary system as a vast irrigation network, with some areas flooded by liquidity while others remain dry. The drawing makes a complex financial system legible, exposing the mechanisms through which money is created, distributed, and concentrated.

This tradition of questioning money and making its hidden dimensions visible continues in the work of three European artists exhibiting at Bitcoin Amsterdam this November. ZETRA, RYR, and Cypherpunk Now draw from graffiti, political printmaking, hacker culture, and early bitcoin communities to explore the changing meaning of money.

Martin Fischer joined the Prague art collective Ztohoven in 2003, a group known for inserting a fictional nuclear explosion into a live Czech Television broadcast. In 2014, the collective opened Paralelní Polis, a hackerspace whose café accepted only bitcoin, and Fischer designed its logo. As he told Bitcoin Magazine’s Aaron van Wirdum in 2020, the arrival of a screen-printing press the following year prompted him to produce his first prints. Since 2020, he has worked under the name Cypherpunk Now, developing a visual record of bitcoin’s evolving culture.

RYR and ZETRA both emerged from Germany’s graffiti scene but approach money from different directions. RYR uses currency itself as material, making paper from shredded banknotes, pigment from their ashes, and concrete grenades filled with shredded cash that he calls “artifacts from the future.” ZETRA, who began painting in the early 1990s and discovered bitcoin in 2017, examines what money can buy. His TOMATOSOUP paintings revisit Andy Warhol’s iconic Campbell’s Soup Cans to chart changing prices in dollars and bitcoin, while THE BIP39 SERIES explores the 2,048 words used in bitcoin wallet recovery phrases, including 1206/NOTE, a collaboration with Polymerbit.

Bitcoin has shaped these artists’ practices, their livelihoods, and the communities around them. Its growing acceptance by banks, investment funds, and corporations has also prompted some difficult questions about the movement’s original ideals and where its culture is heading.

BMAG: Andy Warhol turned Campbell’s soup into an icon of consumer culture, taking an ordinary commodity and elevating it into fine art. Your TOMATOSOUP series returns to that image but introduces something Warhol largely left outside the frame: the changing value of money itself. How did the idea of reworking Warhol’s Campbell’s Soup Cans first come about, and do viewers immediately recognize the commentary on inflation?

ZETRA: We frequently see iPhones and houses in our bitcoin Twitter timelines, showing how they become cheaper in BTC terms. I thought it would be fun to take something from art history instead, something more visually appealing, like Warhol’s iconic Campbell’s Soup Can.

For my TOMATOSOUP painting, I used real stickers placed on the can to show how the price of soup has increased in USD over the past decades, compared with the lower prices we might expect in BTC terms in the decades to come.

Bitcoiners looking at TOMATOSOUP generally understand it immediately. They know they’re in a better position as the purchasing power of fiat money continues to decline through inflation. Other viewers usually need a bit of explanation, and I’m always happy to help them understand.

BMAG: In THE BIP39 SERIES, you draw from the 2,048 words used to generate bitcoin wallet recovery phrases, turning ordinary words into artworks with a deeper significance for bitcoin holders. Can you unpack the different layers of inspiration behind the series and what they reveal about bitcoin, language, and the ownership of money for someone unfamiliar with these concepts?

ZETRA: Everyone who moves their precious sats into cold storage encounters 12 or 24 of these significant words, often early in their journey as a bitcoin newcomer. As mentioned, there are 2,048 words in a carefully curated list representing the power of self-custody.

I started going through the words one by one, imagining how each could be visualized in a physical form: the key visual for the word, its corresponding number, the style, and the medium I would choose. There are millions of possibilities for bringing these words to life through bitcoin art.

1044/LIST was the obvious choice to kick off THE BIP39 SERIES. Naturally, it features all 2,048 words presented as a list. As an ’80s kid, I had to choose 1638/SMILE as the second piece: a proper yellow smiley face, with the number 1638 in place of the eyes. It’s a fine art print on Alu-Dibond beneath a 6 mm acrylic glass cover. So clean.

Another work in the series is 0388/CORN, an obvious homage to Warhol once again. THE BIP39 SERIES will be an ongoing project for many years to come.

BMAG: You shred banknotes into paper and burn them to produce pigment. Artists have long manipulated currency to question where its value resides, but your work goes a step further by making destruction part of the creative process. Is there a contradiction in destroying money to create an artwork that may ultimately be worth much more?

RYR: Money is essentially a narrative system built on collective belief and obedience. It has worked for hundreds of years because we collectively agree on the story it tells and the value it represents. I’ve always been fascinated by that idea, particularly how something as ordinary as a banknote can carry so much meaning, authority, and perceived value.

I was looking for a different way to tell that story, both conceptually and physically. Back in 2017, I had an exhibition title in mind: To Cut a Long Story Short. I liked the cheekiness of it, especially in relation to money and the stories we attach to it. Shredding banknotes became a very literal interpretation of that title, but it also opened up an entirely new artistic medium for me.

Ultimately, I’m not simply destroying money. I’m taking an existing story, cutting it into pieces, and using those pieces to tell a new one.

BMAG: Your concrete weapons are presented as relics from a future in which the fiat wars have already ended. Yet bitcoin is increasingly held through the very financial institutions it was designed to circumvent. Is that a victory for the movement, or have the institutions simply absorbed the alternative?

RYR: I think that’s precisely what makes the story so interesting. When I created the concrete weapons, I imagined a future in which the traditional financial system had already fought its battle for survival. The weapons had become fossils, archaeological artifacts from a monetary conflict that future generations might struggle to understand.

My concrete weapons represent a future in which that battle is already history. Whether bitcoin ultimately wins or becomes part of the very system it challenged remains to be seen.

BMAG: Much of your work is made from the physical remains of money, at a time when currency is becoming increasingly digital and invisible. Do you think people are losing something in their understanding of money as it disappears from everyday physical experience?

RYR: I think we’re losing a physical connection to money, but not necessarily our understanding of it. Money has always been a narrative built on collective trust, whether printed on paper or represented by numbers on a screen. What fascinates me is how something as abstract as value can be represented by a physical object.

I don’t necessarily believe that art has to be authentic or entirely original. Almost everything has been done before. To me, art is a wonderfully human, almost plebeian way of expressing an opinion and giving ideas a physical voice.

Bitcoin will likely evolve into a much broader and increasingly regulated financial asset, but I hope its grassroots culture and artistic identity remain visible. That’s something my fellow artists and I will continue to contribute to, preserving the spirit of a movement that was cultural long before it became institutional.

BMAG: Paralelní Polis wasn’t just a place to discuss alternative monetary systems or a hacker meetup; its café was one of the first to adopt bitcoin as money. What were the early years of Paralelní Polis like, and what has your own experience been selling artwork for bitcoin?

Martin Fischer: Paralelní Polis was founded in 2014, during a bear market. The funny thing is, none of us who founded it even knew what a bear market was. We didn’t think of bitcoin as something that could make us rich. We saw it as uncensorable money and understood the changes it could bring to society. There was no speculation involved, and that’s what made those early days so great.

I sold my first screenprint for bitcoin in 2017, almost ten years ago, and many more since then. But practically every sale was a matter of survival. I spent most of the bitcoin I earned financing my next projects and continuing to make art.

I never managed to accumulate much bitcoin, but looking back, it gave me something far more valuable than investment returns: the freedom to remain an independent artist.

BMAG: Political printmaking has a long history in Europe, from Amsterdam’s financial satires of 1720 to twentieth-century protest posters. Your work emerged from Ztohoven, a collective that famously hacked a live television broadcast to show a fictional nuclear explosion—an audacious intervention, even by today’s standards. Ztohoven challenged institutions through disruption, while bitcoin uses game theory and economic incentives to create an alternative. Do you see bitcoin as a continuation of that same spirit of intervention, and your prints as an extension of it?

Martin Fischer: I think there’s a connection, but I wouldn’t say it’s exactly the same thing. With Ztohoven, we used art to question authority, challenge institutions, and expose how easily reality can be manipulated. Bitcoin doesn’t need to make a statement or provoke anyone. It simply offers an alternative that works without asking anyone for permission. That’s a much more interesting form of disruption to me.

But today, bitcoin has become so corporate and so intertwined with traditional banking that it’s hard to still see it as an anti-establishment movement. I don’t see this as a betrayal of its original ideals, but rather as a natural consequence of its success. That doesn’t mean I like where things are going.

What’s strange is that bitcoin’s fundamental principles haven’t really changed, but the way people perceive and use it certainly has.

And my screenprints? I still work with the original idea of separating money from the state while exploring the myths, memes, and legends of the bitcoin age. That’s what I enjoy most.

BMAG: Your Amsterdam presentation brings together more than a decade of work documenting bitcoin’s evolution from an underground movement to an increasingly institutionalized financial system. Looking across those prints today, has the movement changed more than you expected, or has your own perspective changed? Which of your prints are your favorites?

Martin Fischer: I like remembering the old days, when we were all part of the same tribe and our main enemy was Faketoshi.

Today? We have culture wars over JPEGs, Ordinals, BIPs, OP_RETURN, over what’s spam and what should or shouldn’t belong on bitcoin. What makes me saddest is that people who once fought together against censorship and for freedom now spend enormous amounts of energy fighting each other over what others should or shouldn’t be allowed to do with bitcoin.

Maybe it’s a natural consequence of bitcoin’s success. The bitcoin community has changed enormously, and so has my perspective on it. I’m definitely much more skeptical today of the idea that technology alone can automatically change society for the better.

As for my favorite works, Bitcoin Meteorite is definitely one of them. In this piece, I reworked the meme of banking dinosaurs watching their own extinction, incorporating the abstract from the Bitcoin white paper. It gave me my fifteen minutes of fame when Max Keiser and Stacy Herbert brought it into the spotlight.

Then there’s Cypherpunks of the World. This project is important to me not only as a celebration of the cypherpunks and their legacy, but also because of its complexity. It started as a series of original collages, continued through handmade screenprints, and eventually evolved into animated NFTs and a virtual gallery. It’s one of my most elaborate projects, connecting different techniques and media while staying true to the original idea.

Among my more recent works, I really like Out of Order from 2023. It’s an incredibly detailed screenprint, and the first one where I finally managed to make absolutely no printing mistakes. That alone makes it special to me.

I also love St. Satosius Contra Draconem (2025), which is inspired by the classic depiction of Saint George fighting the dragon, reimagined through bitcoin mythology.

Works by ZETRA, RYR, and Cypherpunk Now, alongside other European artists, will be presented at Bitcoin Amsterdam, November 4–6, 2026, as part of the Bitcoin Museum & Art Gallery (BMAG) programming. Additional artworks and editions will be available through https://shop.museum.b.tc.

Explore more work by the featured artists at ZETRA, RYR, Cypherpunk Now, and www.martin-fischer.cz.

Still, the price of bitcoin rose in September despite the Federal Reserve talking tough on inflation.

Researchers Build First Working Post-Quantum Defense for Bitcoin’s Lightning Network

Whether or not quantum computers will break Bitcoin one day is a hot topic. 

But what about second-layer solutions like Lightning? 

Well, researchers from East Texas A&M University, North American University, Florida Gulf Coast University, and Florida Institute of Technology have been working on that. 

In an announcement Tuesday, the team of researchers said that they built what they describe as the first full post-quantum security design for the Lightning Network.

As first uncovered in a research paper in September, the team said they added post-quantum cryptography to Lightning’s communications, payment requests and related systems, implemented in Rust-Lightning. 

It works like this: The solution layers new quantum-resistant cryptography on top of Lightning’s existing cryptography rather than replacing it. It uses ML-DSA digital signatures and ML-KEM key exchange, post-quantum algorithms standardized by the U.S. National Institute of Standards and Technology, alongside the classical methods Lightning already relies on. 

In this hybrid design, an attacker would have to break both the new and the old cryptography to compromise a connection or forge a payment request.

According to the team led by Dr. Ahmet Kurt, an assistant professor in East Texas A&M’s Department of Computer Science and Information Systems, it took about three to four months and roughly 11,000 lines of code — and it’s a complete working implementation, not just a small demo.

Lightning lets users make fast, cheap Bitcoin payments through a network of off-chain channels instead of recording each one on the blockchain. 

Its cryptography could eventually be broken by powerful quantum computers, and that risk exists even if Bitcoin itself gets upgraded, because Lightning has its own communication and payment systems, the team said. 

They added that their work demonstrates that Lightning’s off-chain systems can begin preparing for the quantum era independently while others focus on solutions for the mainnet. 

Quantum researchers have warned that a time will come when Bitcoin’s software — which underpins the biggest and strongest computer network in the world — will need to be upgraded to deal with quantum computing. 

While some crypto VC firms have urged action, top developers in the space have argued that many of today’s quantum computers have limited capabilities.

Still, they have noted that their development could arrive unexpectedly — just like advances with artificial intelligence — and have started developing some solutions, including top Bitcoin infrastructure firm, Blockstream.

The Amount of Bitcoin on Exchanges Is Shrinking. Is a Rally Imminent?

Bitcoin’s price could be due a move upwards as the supply of the leading cryptocurrency on exchanges shrinks. 

That’s according to a researcher at data firm CryptoQuant, who wrote in a Monday report that bitcoin on exchanges has dropped to 2.67 million from 2.8 million since February. 

The price of bitcoin was recently $83,485, unmoved over a 24-hour period but up 8% over the past 30 days after having its best quarter in years. Its surge in August and September has led a number of analysts to declare the bear market is over.  

“If buying demand continues to improve while exchange supply remains low, BTC could benefit from a supply-demand imbalance, creating favorable conditions for a longer-term upward trend,” the report by on-chain researcher Rei Researcher read. 

It added: “More importantly, in recent weeks, bitcoin has recovered from its lows while exchange reserves have continued to decline. This is a notable development, suggesting that the supply readily available for trading is decreasing even as the market recovers.”

The report further noted that it was possible investors were taking bitcoin off exchanges to put in cold storage solutions. 

Bitcoin’s price was mostly trading under $65,000 for the first half of 2026. The coin spent most of this year in a bear market following the all-time high of $126,080 it hit in October 2025. 

But that all changed in August. News that the U.S. Treasury would double the size of its liquidity-support buyback operations, weakening the dollar but strengthening bitcoin and other non-yield bearing assets. 

Now, the so-called debasement trade — where investors throw money at an asset to hedge against a currency losing its value — is hot again. Bitcoin is benefiting from the trade, analysts say, as it did in 2024 and 2025. 

Bitcoin’s price is still more than 30% below its record.

]]> O Conselho de Estabilidade Financeira (FSB, na sigla inglesa) publicou na segunda-feira (12) um pequeno documento de 5 páginas alertando sobre os riscos das stablecoins.

Embora afirme que o G20 reconheça o papel transformador dessas criptomoedas, o texto também diz ser preciso manter estruturas regulatórias e de supervisão eficazes para continuar promovendo essa inovação enquanto lidam com potenciais vulnerabilidades.

Outro destaque fica para a menção de que 99% dos US$ 300 bilhões do mercado de stablecoins está atrelado ao dólar americano.

Conselho alerta que possíveis problemas com stablecoins podem afetar diversos países

Vistas como um dólar digital, as stablecoins já se consolidaram no mercado de criptomoedas e, cada vez mais, passam a integrar o sistema financeiro tradicional, como em pagamentos diários e transações de remessa.

Em relação a esse ponto, o FSB destaca que, no futuro, as stablecoins podem viabilizar transações domésticas e internacionais em larga escala de maneira mais rápida, transparente e barata.

“A forma como serão utilizadas em cada jurisdição, seja como meio de pagamento, reserva de valor ou ambos, terá possíveis implicações para a natureza e a gravidade das vulnerabilidades que apresentam.”

Como exemplo, o texto cita que, embora as stablecoins possam circular globalmente, os ativos que dão lastro a elas tendem a ficar em um único país. Ou seja, é possível usar uma stablecoin no Brasil, mas o lastro dessa moeda pode estar nos EUA.

Portanto, um problema citado seria os horários em que essas reservas poderiam ser afetadas e exigências regulatórias.

“Em períodos de estresse, o acesso ininterrupto e a velocidade das negociações nos mercados secundários podem aumentar a rapidez e a magnitude das vendas em massa, pressionando a paridade da stablecoin caso os resgates não consigam acompanhar a demanda. Ao mesmo tempo, mercados secundários profundos e líquidos podem facilitar operações de arbitragem que ajudem a estabilizar os preços em torno da paridade.”

Como último alerta, o FSB afirma que uma crise de saques poderia afetar o sistema financeiro tradicional pela venda forçada dessas reservas.

Autoridade afirma ser difícil monitorar movimentações de stablecoins

Embora as transações de stablecoins possam ser vistas por qualquer pessoa, elas são pseudoanônimas, não sendo possível identificar, na maioria das vezes, as partes de uma transferência. Portanto, o FSB aponta para a dificuldade em obter dados confiáveis sobre o mercado.

Isso inclui a atribuição do uso de stablecoins por região.

“A atividade com stablecoins gera uma grande quantidade de dados, mas diversos desafios atualmente limitam sua utilização eficaz no monitoramento de vulnerabilidades à estabilidade financeira. Esses desafios não são igualmente fáceis de resolver. Algumas limitações são estruturais, como o caráter pseudônimo das blockchains públicas, e provavelmente persistirão sem mudanças significativas no ecossistema de criptoativos.”

O texto afirma que as autoridades dependem de empresas privadas especializadas em rastreamento. No entanto, aponta que cada empresa pode utilizar um método diferente, criando riscos ligados tanto à comparação quanto à credibilidade das informações.

A sugestão da autoridade seria que os próprios governos aprofundassem seus conhecimentos em análises. Além disso, também cita a possível exploração de práticas do setor para a coleta de dados tanto on-chain quanto off-chain.

Fonte: FSB alerta para riscos ligados ao mercado de stablecoins, hoje avaliado em US$ 300 bilhões

]]> O Departamento de Justiça dos EUA anunciou nesta terça-feira (13) a prisão de dois indivíduos acusados de facilitar a contratação fraudulenta de trabalhadores da Coreia do Norte em empresas americanas.

A denúncia aponta que eles hospedavam notebooks fornecidos pelas empresas em suas próprias casas para parecer que os norte-coreanos estavam trabalhando fisicamente nos EUA. Além disso, também ajudavam na obtenção de documentos de identidade falsos e também atuavam na parte financeira do esquema.

No mês passado, autoridades japonesas desmantelaram uma ‘fazenda de laptops’ operada por um cidadão local, também com o objetivo de ajudar hackers norte-coreanos.

Governo americano volta a pressionar a Coreia do Norte

As ações da Coreia do Norte estão preocupando tanto especialistas em segurança quanto governos. Como exemplo, o Google publicou em 2025 um estudo apontando que hackers norte-coreanos estão se espalhando pelo mundo, sendo os EUA o país mais afetado.

Já o governo americano aponta que o perigo ainda é maior, já que o objetivo desse esquema é fortalecer os programas armamentistas de seu país inimigo.

John A. Eisenberg, procurador-geral adjunto para Segurança Nacional, destaca que isso poderia ser usado contra os EUA em algum momento.

“O regime desonesto da Coreia do Norte utiliza seus esquemas generalizados de trabalhadores de TI para arrecadar recursos destinados a diversos fins ilícitos, incluindo o desenvolvimento de armas que poderiam, em última instância, atingir os EUA ou seus aliados. Esses esquemas ameaçam a segurança dos sistemas de TI e dos dados dos empregadores americanos enganados, além de deixar inúmeras vítimas de roubo de identidade. A Divisão de Segurança Nacional, juntamente com nossos parceiros de aplicação da lei, utilizará todas as ferramentas disponíveis para localizar qualquer pessoa que esteja ajudando a RPDC e proteger nossa segurança nacional.”

Os dois presos acusados de envolvimento no esquema são Michael James Bostelle, da Pensilvânia, e Juan Cecilio Pena Carrillo, do Texas.

A Justiça americana afirma que a fraude teve início ainda em 2019, gerando mais de US$ 3 milhões em receitas durante o período e afetando 70 empresas americanas.

Outros nomes citados nos processos são os de Sun Sheng Ming, Pei Li Guang, Weng Shou Cheng, Han Guo Bin, Wang Jian Jun, Sheng Zhang Kun, Zhang Wei Ping, Zhang Li Ping, Yu Yang e Jin Long, todos da China. Outros dois suspeitos não tiveram seus nomes revelados.

“Eles também contaram com facilitadores baseados nos EUA, que recebiam e hospedavam vários notebooks fornecidos pelas empresas americanas vítimas do esquema em suas próprias residências, formando as chamadas “fazendas de notebooks”. Esses facilitadores armazenavam e configuravam os dispositivos, instalavam softwares de acesso remoto e transferiam os ganhos para contas controladas pela Coreia do Norte.”

Outro risco seria invasões aos sistemas dessas empresas.

EUA desmantelaram diversas fazendas de notebooks no Texas no mês passado

No mesmo comunicado, o governo americano aponta que o FBI cumpriu em setembro mandados de busca e apreensão em mais de 40 residências no Texas que eram suspeitas de funcionar como fazendas de notebooks para hackers norte-coreanos.

A operação apreendeu cerca de 187 notebooks e outros dispositivos.

No passado, os EUA já haviam realizado outras quatro ações contra a Coreia do Norte.

Finalizando, o texto aponta para recompensas de até US$ 5 milhões por informações que levem à interrupção das atividades financeiras ilícitas da Coreia do Norte.

]]> A Comissão de Valores Mobiliários (CVM) publicou a Resolução 249/2026 nesta quarta-feira (14) para instituir o Programa Piloto DLT e a medida cria um ecossistema de testes focado na emissão, negociação e liquidação de valores mobiliários por meio de redes de registro distribuído.

O regulamento estabelece um ambiente experimental restrito sem envolver recursos financeiros reais ou investidores de varejo nas negociações.

Assim, a autarquia busca avaliar a viabilidade técnica e jurídica da tecnologia sem expor o mercado de capitais aos riscos de falhas operacionais.

O projeto oficializou os esforços do Grupo de Trabalho de Tokenização estruturado pela instituição federal ao longo do ano. O presidente da CVM, Otto Lobo, reforçou a urgência de adaptar a infraestrutura financeira aos novos modelos de negócios.

“A tokenização já está transformando a infraestrutura do mercado de capitais e traz oportunidades relevantes para ampliar a eficiência, a inovação e o acesso a novos modelos de negócios. Cabe à CVM acompanhar esse movimento, testando soluções, dialogando com o mercado, para ter ainda mais subsídios para identificar os caminhos regulatórios mais adequados“, disse.

“A criação do Programa Piloto DLT CVM representa um passo importante para que a Autarquia possa compreender, na prática, as oportunidades, os desafios e os riscos associados ao uso da tecnologia de registro distribuído no mercado de capitais“, seguiu explicando. “Com isso, buscamos criar espaço para a inovação, preservando a segurança, a transparência e a proteção dos investidores“, finalizou Lobo.

Plataformas privadas passarão por auditoria técnica constante e acompanhamento pela CVM

Um cronograma oficial estipula sessenta dias de testes ativos nas redes admitidas, com chance de prorrogação por mais trinta dias.

As equipes gestoras avaliarão a integração entre diferentes plataformas e a segurança cibernética dos contratos inteligentes desenvolvidos para o sistema.

Os construtores das redes precisam fornecer meios de acesso irrestrito para leitura e auditoria das transações pelos técnicos da comissão.

O coordenador do grupo de trabalho destacou a neutralidade do programa diante da pluralidade de soluções disponíveis no mercado global.

“A construção do Programa Piloto DLT CVM contou com ampla escuta de participantes do mercado, que auxiliam o Grupo de Trabalho de Tokenização. Esse diálogo foi fundamental para que o programa fosse abrangente nos testes para diversas tecnologias, preservando, assim, a neutralidade e, ao mesmo tempo, criando espaço para diferentes soluções e futuras inovações no mercado de capitais“, complementou Bruno Gomes, Superintendente de Securitização e Agronegócio da CVM e Coordenador do GTT.

Inteligência artificial apoiará transição para mercado definitivo

A nova resolução dispensa as empresas participantes de cadastros convencionais para a oferta pública durante a fase de simulações em rede.

O corpo técnico concluiu sua primeira missão no prazo exato com a entrega deste arcabouço focado na evolução dos ativos digitais.

Estudos de governança e a estruturação de uma supervisão baseada em ferramentas automatizadas integram os próximos passos das equipes.

O superintendente de desenvolvimento institucional detalhou a sinergia entre o projeto piloto e o uso de inteligência artificial na rotina.

“A CVM está trabalhando para acompanhar e avaliar os testes de ativos tokenizados em diferentes redes, enquanto, paralelamente, avança na análise e seleção de modelos de Inteligência Artificial aplicáveis à supervisão do mercado de capitais. Nosso objetivo é reunir as condições técnicas necessárias para a transição segura do regime experimental para o definitivo, em um processo de constante diálogo com os participantes do mercado e demais atores relevantes“, destacou José Alexandre Vasco, Superintendente Seccional de Desenvolvimento e Modernização Institucional da CVM e Coordenador do GTT.

As associações e entidades interessadas possuem quinze dias úteis para submeter propostas de infraestrutura e gestão de rede ao comitê da comissão. A publicação do relatório final consolidará os resultados obtidos para balizar a formulação de leis perenes para a economia digital no país.

O dinheiro, segundo as autoridades, teria sido usado para bancar uma vida de luxo com carros esportivos, relógios e outros itens, incluindo um diamante raro.

Polícia turca apreendeu diversos equipamentos eletrônicos de Heart

Segundo a mídia local, a polícia turca prendeu tanto Richard Heart quanto sua esposa, identificada pelas iniciais A. K., durante operação realizada nesta quarta-feira (14).

As autoridades encontraram armas de fogo, equipamentos eletrônicos, joias e 600 mil dólares americanos em espécie, além de quantias menores em outras moedas.

Em detalhes, o texto aponta a apreensão de 3 pistolas, 4 rifles de cano longo, 7 carregadores, 1.360 munições e uma adaga. Além disso, 12 celulares, 8 computadores de mesa, 7 notebooks, 20 placas de vídeo, 14 SSDs, 7 pendrives e 3 cartões de memória.

Outros itens apreendidos foram 2 drones, 24 relógios, 20 pulseiras de ouro e 7 colares de corrente de ouro.

Nas redes sociais, Heart era conhecido por ostentar sua vida de luxo antes de começar a ser perseguido pelas autoridades.

Em seu último tuíte antes da prisão, publicado nesta terça-feira (13), o influenciador promovia outra criptomoeda sua, a PulseChain, afirmando que ela seria melhor que a XRP, quinta maior do mercado, devido a uma falha crítica encontrada no projeto.

Criptomoeda de Richard Heart desaba após sua prisão

Embora a Hex já tenha alcançado a marca de US$ 0,5 por unidade em 2021, o projeto, considerado uma possível pirâmide financeira por especialistas, perdeu quase todo o seu valor nos últimos anos e hoje é negociado na faixa dos US$ 0,0005.

Com a prisão do influenciador, a HEX voltou a cair 40% nesta quarta-feira (14). Atualmente, a criptomoeda é negociada somente em corretoras descentralizadas.

Até o momento, não há informações se o influenciador será julgado na Turquia ou extraditado para a Finlândia.

]]> Economista com mais de 1 milhão de livros vendidos cita João Paulo Mayall ao lado de Fidelity e Schwab em defesa do bitcoin https://livecoins.com.br/economista-com-mais-de-1-milhao-de-livros-vendidos-cita-joao-paulo-mayall-ao-lado-de-fidelity-e-schwab-em-defesa-do-bitcoin/ Wed, 14 Oct 2026 15:30:00 +0000 https://livecoins.com.br/?p=198846 Autor de “O Padrão Bitcoin”, traduzido para mais de 35 idiomas, Saifedean Ammous recorre ao cálculo do brasileiro, que mostra o bitcoin oscilando 1,52x o ouro contra 9,4x em 2018, para rebater a tese de que a oferta fixa impede o bitcoin de ser dinheiro

Fonte: Economista com mais de 1 milhão de livros vendidos cita João Paulo Mayall ao lado de Fidelity e Schwab em defesa do bitcoin

Veja mais notícias sobre Bitcoin. Siga o Livecoins no Facebook, Twitter, Instagram e YouTube.

]]> Saifedean Ammous publicou nesta terça-feira (13) uma resposta ao professor Lawrence White, da George Mason University. No livro Better Money, White sustenta que a oferta fixa deixa o bitcoin volátil demais para funcionar como dinheiro.

Para rebater a tese, Ammous reuniu 5 levantamentos, entre eles estudos da Fidelity e da Charles Schwab e o cálculo do empresário João Paulo Mayall, cofundador da QR Capital e responsável pelo QBTC11, primeiro ETF de bitcoin da América Latina, que mostra a volatilidade de 1 ano do bitcoin em apenas 1,52x a do ouro.

O debate

O artigo saiu no X e responde a uma indicação do próprio White. Ammous, que publicou “O Padrão Bitcoin” em 2018 e soma mais de 1 milhão de livros vendidos, tinha afirmado que nunca viu um argumento coerente contra a oferta fixa do bitcoin, e o professor sugeriu o capítulo 6 de Better Money: Gold, Fiat, or Bitcoin?, lançado em 2023 pela Cambridge University Press.

Ammous agradeceu e chamou a obra de primeira tentativa coerente que encontrou de sustentar essa crítica, só que disse continuar não convencido.

A tese de White é que o ouro leva vantagem sobre o bitcoin porque, quando a demanda pelo metal sobe, as mineradoras ampliam a produção e ajudam a segurar o poder de compra. Ammous inverte o argumento.

Se uma oferta que responde à demanda fosse virtude, questiona, o cobre, o ferro ou a prata teriam vencido a competição monetária, já que todos foram dinheiro antes e acabaram substituídos pelo ouro justamente por serem mais fáceis de produzir.

Os números do próprio ouro reforçam o ponto, segundo o economista. Dados do World Gold Council mostram que o estoque de ouro cresceu em média 1,7% ao ano nos últimos 25 anos. Na década de 1970, quando a onça saiu de US$ 35 para US$ 800, a oferta cresceu 1,34% ao ano, e na década seguinte, com o preço recuando para US$ 380, cresceu 1,39%.

Ammous resume a crítica com uma analogia. Atribuir a vitória do ouro à sua pequena elasticidade de oferta, escreve, é como dizer que Usain Bolt venceu os 100 metros porque desacelerou perto da linha de chegada.

Onde entra o dado brasileiro

White escreveu no livro que a volatilidade do bitcoin não caiu à medida que seu valor de mercado cresceu. Para Ammous, a afirmação provavelmente já estava errada quando foi publicada e hoje é muito difícil de sustentar.

É nesse trecho que o economista escreve que J. P. Mayall “mostrou que a volatilidade realizada de 252 dias do bitcoin caiu para apenas 1,52 vez a do ouro”.

O levantamento, publicado pelo brasileiro no X em 7 de outubro, calcula a volatilidade de 1 ano dos 2 ativos desde 2013. Em março de 2018, o bitcoin oscilava 9,4x mais que o ouro. Desde então, a volatilidade do bitcoin caiu de 97,3% para 44,3%, enquanto a do ouro subiu de 10,3% para 29,2%, no ano em que o metal registrou sua maior queda diária desde 1983. Em agosto, a razão entre os 2 chegou a 1,50x, a menor da série.

Mayall antecipou a objeção de que a aproximação se deve à alta da volatilidade do ouro, e não à queda da do bitcoin. Mesmo que o metal voltasse à volatilidade mediana de 2000 a 2024, a distância hoje seria de 3x, menor que qualquer leitura anterior a 2025. “A volatilidade já convergiu, a alocação ainda não”, escreveu J. P. Mayall.

A resposta de Ammous também cita o paper de Kim-Oanh Do na Borsa Istanbul Review, que aponta queda da volatilidade diária e spreads mais estreitos no mercado de bitcoin entre 2012 e 2025, além de um estudo de Huda Aldhahi com dados horários.

Na conclusão do artigo, Ammous afirma esperar que a monetização do bitcoin continue produzindo saldos maiores, mais liquidez e menos volatilidade. Para ele, a volatilidade da fase de transição não descreve o destino.

Os estudos por trás do dado

O cálculo citado por Ammous não é um trabalho isolado.

Cofundador da QR Capital, gestora vendida em 2025, Mayall estruturou o primeiro fundo multimercado 100% em bitcoin do Brasil, em 2020, e o QBTC11, em 2021, além de ter sido responsável por um dos primeiros projetos de tokenização de valores mobiliários aprovados no sandbox regulatório da CVM. Em paralelo, publicou 4 papers no SSRN, a plataforma de pesquisa acadêmica da Elsevier, que formam a base de suas análises sobre moeda, bitcoin e ouro:

  • Bitcoin as Validation of the Regression Theorem: An Austrian Synthesis with Szabo and Ammous, que argumenta que o bitcoin valida o teorema da regressão de Ludwig von Mises e dialoga diretamente com a obra de Ammous. O paper compara ouro, moeda fiduciária e bitcoin em 11 propriedades monetárias, incluindo uma criada por Mayall, a salabilidade prática.
  • The Paradox of Gold Reserves: How Foreign Central Banks’ Gold Holdings Create Indirect Exposure to U.S. Treasuries, que mostra como o ouro guardado por bancos centrais estrangeiros mantém esses países expostos aos Treasuries americanos por 7 canais estruturais, dos quais a repatriação do metal resolve só 1.
  • Inflation: Unraveling the Impact of Monetary Expansion and Interest Rates, escrito com o economista Gerson de Souza Júnior, que trata a inflação como expansão da oferta de moeda, e não como simples alta de preços, comparando EUA e Brasil ao longo de décadas.
  • An Asymmetric Weighted Moving Average for Monetary Aggregates: Evidence from the United States and Brazil, também com Gerson de Souza Júnior, que propõe uma média móvel ponderada assimétrica para medir agregados monetários, com evidências dos EUA e do Brasil.

O julgamento do ouro

Questionado sobre por que reúne tantos argumentos contra o ouro, Mayall conta que os papers são a espinha dorsal de um livro que está por vir, intitulado 5,000 Years Is Enough: The Case Against Gold and the Future of Money, com o subtítulo A Prosecution Through the Lens of the Austrian School of Economics.

“O ouro está sendo desmonetizado, e está repetindo o caminho que a prata fez depois do fim do bimetalismo, em 1873. A prata também foi dinheiro por milênios, até aparecer um dinheiro mais duro. O livro é um julgamento do ouro pelas lentes da Escola Austríaca.”

O projeto também é pessoal. “Minha família acredita no ouro há 6 gerações. Eu fui o primeiro a passar essa convicção pela régua austríaca, e o ouro não sobreviveu ao julgamento”, diz J. P. Mayall.

Isso fez com que o mercado novamente aumentasse as apostas sobre o Fed elevar os juros na próxima reunião, marcada para o dia 29 de outubro.

Como consequência, o Bitcoin opera em queda de 2,1% desde a divulgação dos dados, buscando suporte na região dos US$ 82.000.

Embora o preço do barril de petróleo bruto leve esteja abaixo dos US$ 100, os combustíveis foram um dos itens que mais aceleraram a inflação americana em setembro, após a gasolina subir 9,1% e o óleo combustível 15,3% no mês.

“O índice geral de preços subiu 3,7% nos 12 meses encerrados em setembro, uma alta maior que os 3,4% registrados nos 12 meses encerrados em agosto. O núcleo do índice, que exclui alimentos e energia, subiu 2,6% em um ano, após uma alta de 2,4% nos 12 meses encerrados em agosto. O índice de energia aumentou 20,4% nos 12 meses encerrados em setembro. Já o índice de alimentos subiu 2,5% no último ano.”

Como pode ser visto na imagem acima, a inflação chega a 3,7% nos últimos 12 meses, quase o dobro da meta do Fed de 2%.

Dado isso, o mercado elevou as apostas de que o BC americano voltará a mexer na taxa de juros já na próxima reunião. Ante em 16% de chances, agora o mercado aponta para 40% de probabilidade de um aumento de 0,25 ponto percentual.

Bitcoin e outras criptomoedas operam em queda

Conforme uma taxa de juros mais alta freia a economia e atrai investidores para a renda fixa, tanto o Bitcoin quanto outras criptomoedas operam em queda nesta quarta-feira (14).

Enquanto o Bitcoin cai 2% nas últimas 24 horas, sendo negociado na faixa dos US$ 82.000, o Ethereum perde 3,7% no mesmo período, voltando a operar abaixo dos US$ 2.500. A queda se inicia logo após as 9h30, horário da divulgação dos dados.

Dentre as maiores criptomoedas do mercado, poucas registram ganhos. Os destaques ficam para Tron (TRX), Monero (XMR) e Gram (antiga Toncoin).

Já no mercado de futuros, no entanto, as liquidações não foram altas, ficando em somente US$ 282 milhões nas últimas 24 horas, enquanto menos de 80 mil traders foram liquidados no período.

O estudo recente apontou que as aquisições de stablecoins ultrapassam a metade das compras totais nas grandes corretoras.

Além disso, o crescimento gradual das leis locais aumenta a confiança do mercado na força dessa nova estrutura de liquidação.

Bitcoin holds above $80,000 as Asian stock rout drags altcoins lower

Bitcoin fell to just above $80,000 as South Korea’s Kospi plunged 8%, while the CoinDesk 80 fell 2.2% and all but six CoinDesk 100 members declined.

By Oliver Knight, Omkar Godbole|Edited by Sheldon Reback
Oct 15, 2026, 6:52 a.m. EDT
4 min read

Підсумок
  • Bitcoin fell to just above $80,000 at around 02:30 UTC, close to the Oct. 8 low, before recovering to about $81,200, down around 0.5% since midnight UTC.
  • South Korea’s Kospi plunged 8% and triggered circuit breakers, while Nasdaq 100 index futures slid about 1% and the odds of an October Fed rate hike eased to roughly 26% from a spike near 47%.
  • The CoinDesk 80 slid 2.2% against 0.7% for the CoinDesk 5, and all but six CD100 members were lower.

Bitcoin BTC$80 972,85 is trading at $81,200, down around 0.5% since midnight UTC after trimming a 1% loss from earlier in the session, with buyers stepping in just above $80,000 at around 02:30 UTC, close to the Oct. 8 low of about $80,300.

Asian equities set the tone, with South Korea’s Kospi plunging 8% and triggering circuit breakers while Nasdaq 100 index futures slid about 1%, extending Wednesday’s 1.9% drop in the Nasdaq Composite.

Altcoins took the heavier losses, with ether ETH$2 361,14 down 2.0% near $2,370. The CoinDesk 80 (CD80) slid by 2.2% while the bitcoin-dominant CoinDesk 5 (CD5) lost around 0.7%.

The bigger moves were apparent across lower market cap tokens, with pump.fun PUMP$0.004259 falling by 9.4% as the CoinDesk Memecoin Index lost 4.0%, leaving all but six CD100 members lower.

The odds of an October Federal Reserve interest-rate increase jumped to nearly 47% on CME’s FedWatch after Wednesday’s hotter-than-expected inflation report, from about 22% beforehand. It’s now back to roughly 26%, which leaves Treasury yields and hike pricing as the next signals heading into the U.S. open.

Derivatives positioning

  • Liquidations jumped to nearly $1 billion after a hot inflation print: Nearly $1 billion in crypto futures bets were liquidated over 24 hours as the market wilted after Wednesday's hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation report, up from about $136 million a day earlier. The spike shows how crowded positioning was heading into the data.
  • Ether took a heavier hit than bitcoin: ETH saw more liquidations than bitcoin. Longs worth $200 million were liquidated in ether, significantly more than the $115 million in bitcoin. The difference points to heavier long leverage in ether.
  • Silver outranked a top privacy coin on liquidations: XAG (silver) perpetual futures have seen more liquidations than zcash (ZEC), one of the top privacy coins in a sign of the growing popularity of TradFi assets on crypto platforms.
  • Trading surged while open interest held steady: 24-hour crypto futures volume is $252 billion, up 61% over the period, while open interest (OI) is largely unchanged at $139.6 billion. That means the activity was mostly existing positions being closed or churned, not a big new leverage build. The taker long/short volume ratio is again skewed bearish, with shorts accounting for 51.67% of the flow, little changed from 52% a day earlier.
  • Traders are adding to bitcoin positions as the price falls: BTC's spot price is down over 2% in 24 hours, but notional futures OI is up 1.6%. Because OI is measured in dollars, that implies the number of contracts rose by roughly 3.7%, so net new capital is entering during the drop. The 24-hour OI-adjusted cumulative volume delta (CVD) is negative, alongside negative readings for most coins, so the new money looks more like shorts. OI doesn't show direction, however. BTC's perpetual funding rate is still positive, so longs are still paying to hold.
  • Ether and solana show a similar setup: ETH and SOL futures OI have held largely steady despite bigger spot price drops than bitcoin. Flat dollar OI amid falling prices implies the number of contracts rose by about the size of the price drop, another sign of fresh positions. Both also have negative CVDs and still-positive funding rates.
  • DOGE and NEAR are being de-risked: Their OI drops are far bigger than their spot price declines, which means traders are closing positions and capital is leaving, not just marking down.
  • Bitcoin's implied volatility is holding above 40%: The BVIV index is just above 40% for the second straight day, up from recent lows near 34%. The increase shows renewed demand for options, which remain well short of the panic highs seen in February and June. Ether's volatility index shows a similar pattern.
  • Options flow is two-way in bitcoin and defensive in ether: On Deribit, BTC calls at the $90K and $86K strikes top the 24-hour options volume rankings, while the other three in the top five are puts. Calls above the market point to bets on a rebound, and the puts point to hedging. In ETH's case, puts top the list.

Token talk

  • Pump.fun PUMP$0.004259, the Solana memecoin launchpad token, fell 9.4%, the steepest loss in the CD100, with the broader Solana ecosystem also taking a hit. Jito JTO$0.4551 lost 6.2% and jupiter (JUP) 6.1%, while solana (SOL) slipped only 1.1% to about $103.
  • Pyth network PYTH$0.08523, an oracle token, rose 2.8%, extending a rally that began Oct. 8 after its DAO voted to direct all product revenue into monthly buybacks. CoinMarketCap shows about $96 million of PYTH volume over 24 hours, a 67% increase on the previous 24-hour period.
  • Starknet STRK$0.07692 gained 11%, rebounding after a 17% slide on Oct. 13. It remains 278% higher than its yearly low of $0.021 on Aug. 16.
  • Canton CC$0.1063, the institutional blockchain token, fell 7.3%, optimism OP$0.1288 lost 7.0% and aerodrome (AERO) dropped 6.4%, as a lack of altcoin liquidity continues to weigh on the sector.
  • Larger names held up better, with tron TRX$0.3317 little changed, monero (XMR) down 0.55% and hyperliquid (HYPE) down 0.96% to about $80.

September inflation came in above forecasts and the selloff in AI stocks picked up speed, dragging bitcoin back toward last week’s low.

By Shaurya Malwa

Bitcoin slips under $81,000 after a hot CPI print and a deepening AI selloff

A hotter-than-expected U.S. inflation report briefly lifted bitcoin to nearly $84,000 on Wednesday, then sent it sliding to about $80,400 early Thursday. That’s just above last Thursday’s low of about $80,430. Bitcoin traded under $81,000, down 2.6% over 24 hours.

Core inflation, which strips out food and energy, rose to 2.6% against a 2.5% forecast. A hot print makes another Federal Reserve rate hike more likely, and that tends to lift the dollar and weigh on assets like bitcoin. The Fed meets again on Oct. 27–28.

AI stocks added to the pressure. Nasdaq 100 futures fell 1.2% after Anthropic told prospective investors its revenue grew $16.8 billion in the third quarter, a figure that showed growth slowing.

ZEC led crypto losses, down 11% to about $1,100. Ether dropped 5% to about $2,370, and U.S. spot bitcoin ETFs lost about $261 million on Wednesday, according to SoSoValue data.

A daily close below $80,400 would break the floor buyers have defended twice since last Thursday.

Hyperliquid founder wants U.S. oversight of trading platforms, not his blockchain

Jeff Yan told Bloomberg that U.S. regulatory oversight should apply to the firms using the blockchain, not to the underlying network itself.

By Olivier Acuna|Edited by Sheldon Reback
Oct 15, 2026, 6:00 a.m. EDT
1 min read
Make preferred on
Share this article
X (Twitter)LinkedInFacebookEmail
Make preferred on
Summary
  • Hyperliquid founder Jeff Yan said U.S. regulators should oversee financial firms operating on the blockchain rather than regulate the network itself.
  • Yan’s proposal could allow Wall Street firms to build regulated trading businesses on Hyperliquid without requiring the blockchain to register as an exchange.
  • Kraken parent Payward plans to offer U.S. investors derivatives using Hyperliquid’s technology through a regulated exchange, even as Hyperliquid’s perpetual futures market remains closed to them.

Hyperliquid founder Jeff Yan wants U.S. regulators to oversee financial firms using his blockchain rather than the network itself.

Companies operating trading markets on Hyperliquid should be responsible for meeting regulatory requirements, much like financial firms using internet infrastructure, Yan said Thursday in a Bloomberg interview.

“The regulation sits at the layer where there are controls, and indeed the deployers are the ones that exercise these controls,” Yan said.

Hyperliquid, best known for its eponymous perpetual futures trading platform, remains closed to U.S. customers.

However, Kraken’s parent company, Payward, plans to offer investors in the country derivatives using Hyperliquid’s technology through a regulated exchange. For Hyperliquid, this means it could add a Commodity Futures Trading Commission (CFTC) regulated operator even though its perps market remains unavailable to U.S. customers.

Yan’s proposal would allow Wall Street firms to build trading businesses on Hyperliquid without requiring the blockchain itself to operate as a regulated exchange.

“We’re not trying to displace anything,” Yan said. “In fact, I think the technology can benefit everyone who currently operates markets in a more traditional setting.”

His comments come after President Donald Trump said in August that the CFTC was working to bring Hyperliquid into the U.S. under federal regulations.

Australia’s financial watchdog seeks stiffer rules for crypto exchanges ahead of licensing deadline

The country’s regulator, ASIC, has proposed tougher rules to protect users’ digital assets, crypto trading and to safeguard the country’s financial stability.

By Olivier Acuna|Edited by Omkar Godbole
Oct 15, 2026, 5:53 a.m. EDT
2 min read
Make preferred on
Share this article
X (Twitter)LinkedInFacebookEmail
Make preferred on
Summary
  • Australia’s financial regulator proposed standards requiring cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset custodians to safeguard customer funds, ensure transparent trading and meet financial requirements.
  • The rules take effect April 8, 2027, and existing firms may continue operating if they apply for a license by Oct. 7, 2027, while regulators review their applications.
  • The consultation closes Nov. 27, with final guidance expected in March 2027, as Australia moves to regulate crypto businesses more like traditional financial firms.

Australia's financial regulator proposed new standards for cryptocurrency exchanges and digital asset custodians, setting out how companies must protect customer funds, execute trades and meet financial requirements under laws that take effect next year.

The Australian Securities and Investments Commission (ASIC) said it opened a consultation on the rules on Thursday, which would require affected firms to obtain or update their regulatory approval or license. The consultation closes on Nov. 27, with final guidance and standards expected in March 2027.

The proposals mark the next step in Australia’s effort to bring crypto businesses under the same regulatory framework as traditional financial firms. Parliament passed the legislation in April, joining jurisdictions such as the European Union, Singapore and Hong Kong, which have introduced dedicated crypto regulations.

Australia's move comes years after the 2022 collapse of FTX left about 30,000 Australian customers unable to access their money. Three years earlier, Cryptopia, an exchange in neighboring New Zealand, went bankrupt after a major hack.

The rules take effect on April 8, 2027. Crypto firms already operating in the country have until Oct. 7 of the next year to apply for a license and can continue doing business while ASIC reviews their applications.

For Australian investors, the changes would mean clearer rules on how exchanges hold their assets, execute orders and handle conflicts of interest. Crypto companies would face new compliance obligations and financial requirements to operate legally in the country.

"Our approach is based on the principle of 'same activity, same risk, same regulatory outcome' to align Australia with the approach of comparable overseas jurisdictions," ASIC Commissioner Alan Kirkland said.

Under the consultation paper, platforms would be subject to standards covering the separation and safeguarding of customer assets, trading transparency, settlement procedures and financial resources. The proposed trading rules also address market manipulation, conflicts of interest and how exchanges handle customer orders.

ASIC said it has recorded more than 140 applications from businesses seeking authorization to provide digital asset-related financial services. It also said stablecoins used for payments are being addressed separately through Australia's payment services reforms.

Nearly $1 billion in crypto bets liquidated as bitcoin, ether and XRP slide

Ether accounted for nearly 60% of the forced closures across the two largest cryptocurrencies, falling roughly twice as much as bitcoin.

By Shaurya Malwa
Oct 15, 2026, 12:25 a.m. EDT
2 min read
Make preferred on
Share this article
X (Twitter)LinkedInFacebookEmail
Make preferred on
Summary
  • Nearly $483 million in bitcoin and ether futures positions were liquidated over 24 hours as uncertainty about the Federal Reserve’s next interest-rate decision weighed on cryptocurrency markets.
  • Ether traders bore the brunt of the sell-off, with about $286 million in liquidations as ether fell more than 6 percent to roughly $2,350.
  • Bitcoin declined about 3 percent to around $81,000, while losses spread to smaller tokens including Solana, dogecoin and Zcash.

Nearly $483 million in bitcoin and ether futures positions were closed over the past 24 hours as cryptocurrency prices fell Thursday, with ether traders taking the largest hit.

Crypto losses worsened on Thursday morning as uncertainty over the Federal Reserve’s next interest-rate decision weighed on markets. Bitcoin traded around $81,000, down roughly 3% over 24 hours, while ether lost more than 6% to about $2,350. XRP and Solana’s SOL fell around 5%, and dogecoin dropped roughly 6%.

Ether contracts accounted for about $286 million of liquidations, compared with $197 million for bitcoin, according to CoinGlass data checked during Asian morning hours. Ether fell about 6.4% to $2,356, while bitcoin lost roughly 3.2% to trade around $81,000.

Liquidations happen when traders use borrowed money and a price move leaves them without enough collateral to keep their bets open. The exchange closes the position automatically. Someone using $1,000 to control a $10,000 position, for example, can lose their backing on a move of less than 10% against them.

Those closures can add pressure to a falling market, forcing traders out regardless of whether they wanted to sell at that price.

Ether’s damage was larger even though its futures market is considerably smaller.

Outstanding ether contracts totaled about $30 billion, against $52 billion for bitcoin. The liquidation figures measure the value of positions closed, rather than the cash traders personally lost.

The selling reached smaller tokens too. Solana futures recorded about $31 million in liquidations as SOL fell roughly 5.5%. Zcash contracts added nearly $19 million, with ZEC dropping about 13%.

Bitcoin mining pool once handling 2.3% of network shuts after hashrate falls 65%

Computing power directed at Binance Pool has fallen from 26 EH/s in December to about 9 EH/s. Its remaining miners must choose another provider before a Nov. 10 cutoff.

By Shaurya Malwa
Oct 15, 2026, 12:13 a.m. EDT
3 min read
Make preferred on
Share this article
X (Twitter)LinkedInFacebookEmail
Make preferred on
Summary
  • Binance will close its bitcoin mining pool and related services on Nov. 10, giving miners about four weeks to move their computing power elsewhere.
  • Binance Pool’s computing power has fallen about 65% since December, to roughly 9.2 exahashes per second, or less than 1% of Bitcoin’s network.
  • The closure follows other industry exits and could further concentrate block production among Foundry USA, AntPool and F2Pool, which together control about 64% of the network’s computing power.

Crypto exchange Binance is shutting the bitcoin mining pool it launched in April 2020, with the computing power directed at the service down nearly two-thirds from the end of last year.

Binance Pool had an estimated 26 exahashes per second, or 2.3% of Bitcoin’s network, in December, according to Hashrate Index. Its latest table puts the pool at about 9.2 EH/s, under 1% and ranking 11th. That works out to a decline of roughly 65%.

One exahash per second is a quintillion guesses every second at the puzzle that earns a bitcoin block. A mining pool combines work from many machines so their owners receive regular payments instead of waiting to find a block alone.

Binance used a payout model known as full pay-per-share, or FPPS, paying miners for their work and taking on the risk that the pool found fewer blocks than expected.

The exchange said earlier this week that Binance Pool, Pool Savings, Cloud Mining, its transaction accelerator and related services will close at 7 a.m. UTC on Nov. 10, citing an ongoing review of its products and services. It gave no financial explanation for the decision.

Miners have about four weeks to direct their machines elsewhere. After the cutoff, Binance will stop crediting mining shares, the records of work used to calculate payouts. Pool Savings users must redeem their positions, while anyone awaiting a final payout should complete required identity checks by 11:59 p.m. UTC that day.

Pool pages will disappear permanently on Nov. 24, giving customers another two weeks to download records and check payout status.

Four years ago, Binance was offering to finance miners’ expansion. In October 2022, it announced a $500 million lending program through the pool, offering secured loans for 18 to 24 months at interest rates of 5% to 10%. The closure notice does not address that program or disclose any outstanding loan balance.

Fewer pools to choose from

Binance follows SBI Crypto, which shut its pool on July 31 after accounting for roughly 2% of Bitcoin’s computing power. Crypto exchange OKX ended its mining pool services in February 2024.

Hashrate Index’s December report described Binance Pool as the last surviving pool from the period when exchanges expanded into mining.

Read More: SBI Crypto to shut down mining pool that holds roughly 2% of Bitcoin’s hashrate

Poolin, once the largest pool with nearly a fifth of global hashrate, also filed for bankruptcy in July owing about $173 million. Its troubles involved frozen wallet funds and stalled Texas mining sites, and its pool share had already been near zero for years.

The largest pools now account for a greater share of block production. Foundry USA, AntPool and F2Pool together represented about 64.2% in Hashrate Index’s latest table. December’s three largest held 61.4%, with ViaBTC occupying third place instead of F2Pool.

Traditional pool operators choose which transactions their participating machines work to confirm. Closing pools therefore narrow miners’ choice of providers in a business that influences which bitcoin payments get included in blocks. Miners can redirect their machines to smaller providers, however, and pool shares do not establish ownership of the hardware.

If all of Binance’s remaining computing power moves to the three largest pools, their combined share would reach roughly 65%, assuming the rest of the network stays unchanged. Binance has not identified where its remaining miners will go.

Live updates: Bitcoin falls back to $82,000 after inflation rises more than forecast

An historic turnaround lower in interest rates suggests the possibility that the bond bear market may have run its course.

Remarkable bond market turnaround could signal next leg up for crypto

The U.S. 10-year Treasury yield is trading lower by 2.6 basis points at 5.191% shortly after the close of U.S. stocks.

In the wake of the hot inflation report this morning, it had risen as high as 5.36%.

How rare is that sort of turnaround? According to Bespoke, it’s the first time since December 2022 that the 10-year yield rose 10 or more basis points and then fell 10 or more basis points from that intraday high to finish lower on the day.

What’s it mean? No one knows for sure, but in the old commodity pits, these sorts of “outside days” often signaled key trend reversals. If, in fact, the long run higher in interest rates has run its course, risk assets — crypto obviously included — could stand to benefit.

Fed's Goolsbee: Inflation numbers 'discouraging,' but need more data

This morning’s stronger-than-forecast CPI report was “discouraging,” said Austan Goolsbee, president of the Chicago Fed.

“We need to get more data,” before moving to again hike rates, Goolsbee told Yahoo Finance.

It’s important to focus on the trend of inflation, he said, rather than one report.

Losses accelerate in mid-afternoon trading, sending crypto stocks sharply lower

The Nasdaq has extended its decline to more than 2%, a bit more than 90 minutes before the close of trading.

Apart from Apple, which is showing a small gain, the Mag 7 names are lower across the board, led by Nvidia’s and Meta’s 3.3% declines. Tesla is off 2.7%, and Amazon is down 2%.

Bitcoin is near session lows at $81,500, down 2% over the past 24 hours.

Among crypto decliners: Coinbase COIN -5.3%, Robinhood HOOD -8.9%, Bullish BLSH -5.1%, Circle CRCL -6.7%, Galaxy Digital GLXY -9%, and Strategy MSTR -6%.

Can’t blame bond yields. The 10-year U.S. Treasury is now lower by 3 basis points to 5.18% despite the disappointing inflation report, as money flows out of equities and into fixed income.

Bond vigilantes blink as cracks appear in markets

After surging higher in a knee-jerk response to the worse-than-expected U.S. September CPI report, bond yields are barely higher in early afternoon trading.

At 5.23%, the U.S. 10-year yield — after rising to 5.335% — has returned to the low end of its recent range, higher by less than two basis points on the day. The 2-year note has reversed similarly.

Money is moving into fixed income as stocks tumble, with the Nasdaq down 1.6% and the S&P 500 off 1.05%.

The action in tech favorites, homebuilders, and financials, among others, suggests an economy beginning to show some strain from the relentless march higher in interest rates of the past few months.

Bitcoin has edged off session lows, now down 1.5% over the past 24 hours at $81,950.

S&P 500 on pace for first 1% decline in nearly three months

Amid the inflation/interest rate scare and poor earnings from Bank of America, the S&P 500 is lower by more than 1% just after the noon hour on the East Coast.

Stocks fluctuate, so it’s not that notable of a move except for the fact that the S&P hasn’t had a full-day 1% decline since late July, noted Eddy Elfenbein.

The Nasdaq is down 1.6%. The DJIA is down just 0.3% as defensive health care and consumer staples stocks rise.

Neoclouds continue to tumble as rates and concern over CoreWeave surge

“The neocloud massacre continues,” writes Shay Boloor, chief market strategist at Futurum Securities.

CoreWeave (CRWC) is leading the way, down 15% amid concerns about its equity after the yield on its 2032 bonds reached as high as 15% yesterday.

“Yikes,” said Elon Musk.

“It’s not that supercomputer data centers are not in high demand, as they definitely are,” he later added. “However, getting money to build complex hardware systems with massive power, cooling & networking is not the same as doing it.”

Among those also plunging again on Wednesday: Hut 8 HUT and TeraWulf WULF, each down 10%, and Core Scientific CORZ, IREN IREN, and Bitdeer (BTDR), each down 9%.

To take a couple of examples over longer periods, HUT remains higher by nearly 50% year-to-date, but is now down almost 50% since topping out four months ago. IREN, which soared from about $5 per share in 2025 to above $70 at one point this year, is down about 60% from four months ago.

“The issue for several of the neoclouds is that they have locked in the income side on contracts, but have open risk on building costs and financing costs, which are going up,” said Andreas Steno Larsen.

One key Kevin Warsh metric improved in September CPI

In Kevin Warsh’s surprisingly hawkish Jackson Hole speech in late August, the Fed chair said he favored one rarely-mentioned inflation gauge — the PCE diffusion metric, i.e., the share of PCE components rising more than 3%. He noted in that speech that this diffusion gauge was above 50%, suggesting a broadening in inflation.

Anna Wong, chief U.S. economist at Bloomberg, took a similar look at the CPI diffusion in this morning’s report. She found that the share of CPI components rising by more than 3% is actually declining on both a six-month and an annualized basis, with both under 50%.

The energy shock in a chart

“The entire [inflation] impact comes from refined products,” writes economist Daniel Lacalle.

His accompanying chart showing CPI categories is an interesting one, with fuel oil prices higher by 74.2% year-over-year, gasoline up 34.2%, and airline fares up 22.4%.

Prices for most other day-to-day items are far more contained.

“Rate hikes will not create more barrels nor increase refining, but they damage families and businesses,” concluded Lacalle.

Session lows across the board, with bitcoin sliding below $82,000

A modest attempt at an early bounce has failed a bit less than an hour into the U.S. trading session, with crypto prices and stocks all at session lows.

The moves come following an ugly September CPI report that showed headline and core inflation both back on rise, while real wages fall. The Fed will likely find itself forced to hike rates — perhaps multiple times — even as employment growth is slowing and the unemployment rate has begun to rise.

Trading near $84,000 at one point overnight, bitcoin has pulled back to $81,900, down 1.8% over the past 24 hours. Ether, solana, and XRP are down closer to 3%.

The Nasdaq is lower by 0.9%, with Apple helping prop that index with a 1.2% advance. The S&P 500 is off 0.65%, led by Bank of America’s post-earnings 7% decline.

Bond prices are paring some declines, though remain sharply lower for the day. The 10-year U.S. Treasury yield is higher by 5 basis points to 5.27% after earlier rising as high as 5.33%.

BlackRock's crypto assets rebound to nearly $80 billion, but remain down 23% from last year

BlackRock's digital asset products attracted $7.9 billion in net inflows during the third quarter, according to the asset manager’s latest earnings release, reversing roughly $2.2 billion in outflows during the first half of 2026.

The inflows helped lift the firm's digital asset assets under management by 63% to $79.6 billion, up from $48.8 billion at the end of June.

Still, those assets remain 23% below the $104 billion BlackRock managed a year earlier.

Most of the quarterly increase came from rising crypto prices, which added $22.9 billion to asset values.

BlackRock also generated $39 million in quarterly fees from its digital asset products, according to its earnings report.

'Energy shock is spreading': Economist breaks down CPI report

“This is a rough September inflation report,” said Heather Long, chief economist at Navy Federal Credit Union.

The 0.6% rise in headline CPI was the largest jump since May, she noted.

Core inflation, meanwhile, is running at well above a 3% annualized pace over the past three months … “that’s problematic,” Long said.

And year-over-year inflation at 3.7% is wiping out wage gains of 3%.

While high gasoline and diesel prices are the major driver, she concluded, big jumps in airfares, used car prices, recreation, medical, and apparel mean “the energy shock is spreading.”

October Fed rate hike odds just doubled

Following weak employment data and a string of dovish comments from Fed speakers over the past two weeks, markets had more or less written off the chance of a rate hike when the central bank next meets on October 27/28.

But after this morning’s inflation data — particularly at the core level, where CPI rose 0.3% versus 0.2% expected, and 2.6% year-over-year versus 2.5% expected — traders are pricing in a 44% chance the Fed hikes in two weeks, per CME FedWatch.

The odds of two rate hikes by year-end have soared to 44% from just 13% one week ago.

Hot inflation report puts multiple Fed rate hikes back in play

U.S. inflation sped up more than expected in September, perhaps putting multiple Federal Reserve rate hikes back into play.

The September Consumer Price Index rose 0.6%, according to a Wednesday morning report from the Bureau of Labor Statistics. That’s up from 0.4% in August, and in line with economist forecasts for 0.6%.

On a year-over-year basis, however, CPI rose 3.7% versus 3.4% in August and above estimates for 3.6%.

Core CPI — which strips out food and energy costs — also disappointed, rising 0.3% in September. That was the same pace as August, but above consensus forecasts for 0.2%.

Year-over-year core CPI was higher by 2.6% versus 2.4% the previous month and above estimates for 2.5%.

Bitcoin BTC$80,972.85 dropped $1,000 on the news, now trading at $82,800.

The bond market is getting crushed, the 10-year U.S. Treasury yield jumping 9.3 basis points to 5.308%, and the 2-year yield soaring 13.1 basis points to 4.924%.

Nasdaq 100 futures are lower by 0.65% and S&P 500 futures by 0.3%. Gold has slumped 1.5% to $4,116 per ounce.

Ahead of the data, a string of Fed speakers had hinted that the central bank was likely to raise interest rates another 25 basis points before year-end. Market pricing reflected that information, with most expecting the central bank to pause at its upcoming meeting later this month, but hike at its final meeting of the year in early December.

This morning’s numbers just might put an October rate hike back on the table.

Treasury yields ease to 5.20% before inflation data

Treasuries extended their rebound on Wednesday ahead of the September U.S. inflation report, pulling the 10-year yield down one basis point to 5.20%. That’s down from about 5.32% last week, when it hovered near its highest since 2002.

Forecasts point to the report showing underlying prices, which strip out volatile food and energy costs, rising more slowly than in August. A softer reading would ease pressure on the Federal Reserve to keep raising rates, and bitcoin has been held back by those rate fears all month.

Bitcoin needs real buyers, not short covering, to climb back, eToro says

Bitcoin sat near $83,200 on Wednesday, 34% below the record above $126,000 it set a year ago. Traders were holding back ahead of U.S. inflation data, and chip stocks looked set for a sixth day of losses.

A lasting recovery “will require genuine buying demand, not just short covering,” said Javier Molina, a market analyst at eToro. Short covering is when traders who bet on a decline buy back to close their positions. It can lift prices fast, but it fades once those bets are closed.

Molina said spot bitcoin ETFs have opened the asset to big investors but haven’t shielded it from interest rates, the dollar or liquidity.

Bitcoin knocked back from $84,000 as the Nasdaq holds it on a short leash

A brief spike to $84,000 early Wednesday faded within the hour, leaving bitcoin down 0.5% at about $83,200. It’s still boxed between its 50-day moving average near $81,000 and a ceiling at $84,000.

The 50-day moving average is bitcoin’s average closing price over the past 50 days, and traders watch it for the medium-term trend. Buyers defended it on Tuesday, when bitcoin bottomed near $81,000, but they haven’t managed to push the price through $84,000 since.

ZEC and TRX were the only gainers among the majors, up about 1%. HYPE was the laggard, down 2% to about $81. SOL fell 1.4% and ether slipped 1% to just under $2,500, according to CoinDesk data.

Bitcoin trades close to the Nasdaq 100 in how institutions rank risk, and “the latter’s caution is preventing Bitcoin from spreading its wings,” said Alex Kuptsikevich, chief market analyst at FxPro.

Nasdaq 100 futures were little changed, and an ETF tracking chipmakers pointed to another day of selling even after ASML rose more than 2% in Europe. The chip-equipment maker said it can’t fully meet demand for the next two years. Bank of America and Morgan Stanley report later Wednesday, and forecasts point to the September U.S. inflation report showing a slowdown in underlying prices.

A daily close above $84,000 would be the first sign that buyers have broken out of the range.
